title: How a vacuum tube switches: diodes, triodes and flip-flops
text:
CHAPTER 4. VACUUM TUBES AND THE FIRST ELECTRONIC COMPUTERS
SECTION 4.1. HOW A VACUUM TUBE SWITCHES: DIODES, TRIODES AND FLIP-FLOPS

Relays move metal; vacuum tubes move only electrons. Removing the moving parts made switching roughly a thousand times faster, and that speed-up is the reason the first electronic computers, Colossus and ENIAC, could do in seconds what relay machines needed hours for. This section explains, at the level of device physics and circuits, how a vacuum tube works as an amplifier and as a switch, how tubes are combined into logic gates, and how two tubes cross-coupled form a flip-flop, the basic memory cell of every digital computer since.

1. Thermionic emission

When a metal is heated, some electrons gain enough thermal energy to escape its surface. Thomas Edison noticed a related effect in his light bulb experiments in the 1880s (current flowing in a vacuum from the hot filament to a separate electrode), and the physics was worked out in the early twentieth century by Owen Richardson, who received the 1928 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

The emitted current density follows the Richardson-Dushman law:

    J = A * T^2 * exp( -W / (k * T) )

where J is the current density (A/m^2), T the absolute temperature (K), W the work function of the metal (the energy needed to free an electron, typically a few electron-volts), k Boltzmann's constant, and A a constant of the material. The exponential means emission is extremely sensitive to temperature and work function. That is why practical tubes used cathodes coated with oxides of barium and strontium, which have a low work function and emit well at a dull red heat, rather than bare tungsten that had to run white hot.

A tube needs a heater to keep its cathode hot, and that heater is one of the central engineering facts of tube computing: every tube consumed watts of power continuously just to stay ready, whether it was switching or not, and heaters were the part that wore out.

2. The diode

John Ambrose Fleming patented the thermionic diode, the "Fleming valve," in 1904, originally as a detector for radio signals. It has two electrodes in an evacuated glass envelope:

  - the cathode (heated, emits electrons);
  - the anode, also called the plate (collects electrons when it is positive relative to the cathode).

If the plate is positive, electrons flow from cathode to plate and current flows (conventional current, plate to cathode). If the plate is negative, it repels electrons and no current flows. The diode is a one-way valve for current, which is why the British call tubes "valves."

The current is limited by the cloud of electrons near the cathode (the space charge). For an ideal planar diode, the Child-Langmuir law gives:

    I = K * V^(3/2)

where V is the plate voltage and K depends on geometry. The current rises with a three-halves power of voltage, not linearly as in a resistor.

Diodes as logic. Diodes alone can build AND and OR gates (diode logic). An OR gate: connect each input through a diode to a common output node with a resistor to ground. If any input is high, its diode conducts and pulls the output high. An AND gate: connect each input through a diode (reversed) to a node pulled up to the supply through a resistor; if any input is low, it pulls the node low, so the output is high only if all inputs are high. Diode logic cannot invert and loses signal level through each stage, so it needs amplifying elements as well. Later computers used crystal (semiconductor) diodes for much of their logic, combined with tubes for inversion and amplification.

3. The triode

In 1906 Lee de Forest added a third electrode to the diode, creating the Audion, which developed into the triode. The third electrode, the control grid, is a fine wire mesh between cathode and plate. (De Forest did not at first fully understand how his device worked; others, notably at General Electric and AT&T, developed the high-vacuum triode into a reliable amplifier in the 1910s.)

The grid is close to the cathode, so a small voltage on it has a large effect on the electric field the electrons feel. Make the grid negative and it repels electrons back toward the cathode, reducing plate current; make it sufficiently negative and the current is cut off entirely. Because the grid is held negative, it attracts almost no electrons, so it draws almost no current: the control is by voltage, with very little input power. That is the essence of amplification.

A useful approximate model for the plate current is:

    Ip = K * (Vg + Vp / mu)^(3/2)     when (Vg + Vp / mu) > 0
    Ip = 0                            otherwise (cut off)

where Vg is the grid-to-cathode voltage, Vp the plate-to-cathode voltage, and mu the amplification factor (typically from about 5 to 100 depending on the tube). This says the grid is mu times more effective than the plate at controlling current.

Small-signal parameters, which you can compare later with the transistor's:

    transconductance gm = dIp / dVg   (typically a few mA per volt)
    plate resistance rp = dVp / dIp
    and mu = gm * rp

4. The triode as an amplifier and inverter

Connect the plate to a supply voltage V+ (say 250 V) through a load resistor RL, put the cathode at ground, and apply the input to the grid. The output is taken at the plate.

    Vout = V+ - Ip * RL

  - When the grid is very negative (input "low"), Ip = 0, so Vout = V+, high.
  - When the grid is near 0 V (input "high"), a large Ip flows, the drop across RL is large, so Vout is low.

So a triode with a plate resistor is an inverter: low in gives high out and vice versa. Used in its linear region it is an inverting amplifier with voltage gain roughly:

    Av = - mu * RL / (rp + RL)

For digital use, engineers deliberately drove tubes hard between two states: fully cut off and fully conducting. This switching mode is tolerant of variation between tubes, which mattered greatly when a computer used thousands of them, each slightly different and drifting with age. The logic levels were wide voltage ranges rather than precise values.

Because the plate is at a high positive voltage and the grid needs a negative voltage to cut off, connecting one stage's output to the next stage's grid needs level shifting, typically a resistor divider to a negative supply. Tube computers therefore needed several supply voltages and careful design of these coupling networks.

5. More grids: tetrodes and pentodes

Adding a screen grid (tetrode) between control grid and plate reduces the capacitance between grid and plate, which otherwise limits high-frequency performance. Adding a suppressor grid (pentode) solves a problem of secondary electrons knocked off the plate. Some pentodes have two separately controllable grids, so the plate current flows only when both are positive enough: a single tube that computes AND. Several early computers used such multigrid tubes as gates.

6. Speed

Why is a tube so much faster than a relay? Electrons crossing a gap of a millimeter or so under hundreds of volts reach high speed and take on the order of nanoseconds. In practice the switching time of tube circuits was set not by electron transit but by stray capacitance charging through load resistors: the RC time constant. With load resistances of thousands of ohms and stray capacitances of tens of picofarads, time constants were around a fraction of a microsecond. Typical tube computers ran with pulse rates from about 100 kHz to a few MHz. ENIAC's basic clock was 100 kHz. Compare a relay at perhaps tens to hundreds of operations per second: a factor of a thousand or more.

7. The flip-flop: memory from two tubes

In 1918 the British physicists William Eccles and F. W. Jordan invented a circuit with two triodes, each one's plate coupled to the other's grid. They called it a trigger relay; we call it the Eccles-Jordan flip-flop, or bistable multivibrator.

How it works. Take two inverters, A and B. Connect the output of A to the input of B and the output of B to the input of A.

    Suppose A is conducting: A's plate is low.
    A's low plate drives B's grid negative: B is cut off.
    B's plate is therefore high.
    B's high plate drives A's grid positive: A stays conducting.

The state is self-sustaining. The mirror-image state (B conducting, A cut off) is equally stable. The circuit has two stable states and so stores one bit, for as long as power is applied. A pulse applied to the appropriate grid flips it from one state to the other.

In Boolean terms, two cross-coupled NOR or NAND gates form a set-reset latch:

    Q    = NOT (R OR Qbar)
    Qbar = NOT (S OR Q)

  - S = 1 forces Q = 1 (set).
  - R = 1 forces Q = 0 (reset).
  - S = R = 0 leaves the stored value unchanged.

This is exactly the relay seal-in circuit of Section 2.1 in electronic form, but switching in microseconds instead of milliseconds. Every register in every processor you will ever use is built from this idea, now with transistors.

8. Counting with flip-flops

Arrange a flip-flop so that each input pulse toggles it. It then outputs one transition for every two input pulses: it divides by two. Chain such toggle flip-flops and each one divides by two again, forming a binary counter. Their states read as a binary number of pulses received:

    pulses:  0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8
    Q2 Q1 Q0: 000 001 010 011 100 101 110 111 000

This idea came from physics labs. In the early 1930s at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, C. E. Wynn-Williams built "scale-of-two" counters with gas-filled thyratron tubes to count particles from radioactive decay, which were too fast to count with mechanical counters. This is often cited as one of the first uses of electronic binary counting. Nuclear physics instrumentation of the 1930s thus supplied the circuit vocabulary of the first electronic computers.

ENIAC used a decimal variant: rings of ten flip-flops per digit, with exactly one flip-flop "on," passing the on-state along with each pulse (a ring counter), as we will see in Section 4.3.

9. The reliability problem and how it was solved

Tubes failed. Heaters burned out, cathodes lost their emission, glass envelopes cracked, and failures were most common when tubes were switched on and the heater experienced thermal shock. With thousands of tubes, a machine might expect a failure every few hours or days unless designed carefully. Critics doubted that machines like Colossus (about 1,600 tubes in the first model) or ENIAC (about 18,000) could ever work.

The engineers' answers, which Tommy Flowers (Colossus) and J. Presper Eckert (ENIAC) both applied, were practical:

  - Run heaters below their rated voltage, and run tubes at reduced currents and voltages, which greatly lengthens tube life.
  - Leave the machine powered on continuously, to avoid the thermal shock of switching on and off.
  - Choose and screen tubes, using types with good track records; Flowers's experience came from telephone switching equipment built with valves.
  - Use digital switching operation, so a weakening tube still works correctly until it is far gone.
  - Design for maintenance: plug-in units that could be replaced quickly and diagnostic procedures to find faulty tubes.

These are still the principles of reliable engineering design: derate components, minimize stress, design for graceful degradation and for maintainability.

10. Cost of the tube era

A tube is large (centimeters), uses watts of heater power, needs high voltages, and costs real money. A computer of the late 1940s with a few thousand tubes filled a room, consumed tens to hundreds of kilowatts, and needed serious cooling. Memory was the hardest problem: a bit stored in a tube flip-flop cost one to two tubes, so main memory had to be built from other technologies such as mercury delay lines, cathode-ray tube storage (Williams tubes), magnetic drums and later magnetic cores (Section 4.4 and Section 5.4). The transistor (Chapter 5) solved the tube's basic problems of power, size and heat while keeping its electronic speed, and the integrated circuit (Chapter 6) put many transistors on one chip.

11. Summary

  - Heated cathodes emit electrons (thermionic emission, J = A T^2 exp(-W/kT)); a diode (Fleming, 1904) passes current only when the plate is positive.
  - The triode (de Forest's Audion, 1906, developed into a reliable high-vacuum device in the 1910s) controls plate current with a grid voltage, Ip = K (Vg + Vp/mu)^(3/2), allowing amplification with almost no grid current.
  - A triode with a plate resistor is an inverter; driven between cutoff and full conduction it is a fast digital switch, with speed limited by RC time constants to around a microsecond or less.
  - Two cross-coupled tubes form the Eccles-Jordan flip-flop (1918), a one-bit memory; chains of toggle flip-flops count in binary, an idea used in 1930s particle counters.
  - Reliability of thousands of tubes was achieved by derating, continuous operation and maintainable design; power, heat and memory cost remained the tube era's main limits.
